mainTopic: אותו ואת בנו: including כלאים through או, and whether the איסור applies to males
overview: The גמרא asks whether the איסור of אותו ואת בנו (slaughtering an animal and its offspring on the same day) applies to כלאים, a cross between a sheep and a goat. רבא teaches that the word שה always leaves out כלאים. The גמרא answers that the extra word או in the פסוק brings it back in. The גמרא defends this twice: the teaching that each animal counts on its own comes from בנו, and the ברייתא's teaching comes from אותו. For חנניה, who uses אותו for something else, no פסוק is needed, because he holds like רבי יונתן. A ברייתא about cursing one's father and mother shows that for רבי יונתן, 'and' already means each one alone. The גמרא then explains the מחלוקת: the רבנן say אותו ואת בנו applies only to females, while חנניה says it applies to males too. The רבנן learn their view from a comparison to שילוח הקן, backed up by the word אותו (one parent, not two). The word בנו shows that this one parent is the mother, whom the young follows.

steps.title: The paradigm: the word שה excludes mixed breeds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes quoting רבא, whose words began at the end of the last amud: the word שה in the Torah always comes to exclude כלאים, so אותו ואת בנו should not apply to כלאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: This פסוק sets a pattern: anywhere the תורה says 'שה,' it comes only to leave out the mixed breed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting רבא, who says the word שה always leaves out a כלאים animal. This works as a challenge to anyone who says אותו ואת בנו applies to כלאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק of אותו ואת בנו uses the word שה. If שה always excludes כלאים, then a כלאים animal and its offspring should be allowed to be slaughtered on the same day. The גמרא now needs a source that brings כלאים back in.

keyTerms.meaning: Set up a general pattern from one פסוק that applies everywhere else
A sheep or a goat
A mixed breed, here the offspring of a sheep and a goat
To exclude, to leave out

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is starting in the middle of a quote. The words 'this established a paradigm' are רבא's. The last amud ends 'ועוד, שה כתיב, ואמר רבא', so this is the rest of that second challenge, not a ברייתא.

phrases.english: This established a paradigm:
phrases.notes: This refers to the פסוק listing the kosher animals (דברים 14:4), which says 'שה' of sheep and 'שה' of goats.

phrases.english: wherever 'seh' is stated,
it comes only to exclude the mixed breed.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה בָּנָה אָב כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר שֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא quoted before this section, which challenges applying אותו ואת בנו to כלאים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that אותו ואת בנו applies to כלאים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק of אותו ואת בנו says שה, and שה always excludes כלאים.

steps.title: The word 'or' brings the mixed breed back in
steps.stepSummary: The word או in the פסוק of אותו ואת בנו is extra, and it comes to include כלאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'or' in order to include the mixed breed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק of אותו ואת בנו has an extra word, או ('or'), and that word comes to include כלאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word שה on its own would leave out כלאים. But the פסוק says 'שור או שה', and the extra או is read as a רבוי that adds כלאים back in. So the איסור of אותו ואת בנו does apply to כלאים.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Or,' here read as an extra word
To include, to add something in

phrases.english: The verse says 'or'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 22:28: 'whether it be a bull or a sheep, it and its offspring.'

phrases.english: to include the mixed breed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קְרָא אוֹ לְרַבּוֹת אֶת הַכִּלְאַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the paradigm of שה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to an extra word in the פסוק that overrides the general rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because of the word שה, כלאים would be left out.
steps.terutzMaskana: The extra או includes כלאים in אותו ואת בנו.

steps.title: 'Or' is needed to make each animal count separately
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: או is not extra, because it teaches that a bull with its offspring, or a sheep with its offspring, is each enough for liability.
steps.simpleTranslation: This 'or' is needed to separate. Otherwise you might think a person is not liable until he slaughters a bull with its offspring and also a sheep with its offspring. So 'or' teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer. It says the word או already has another job, so it cannot also be used to include כלאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without או, one might think the תורה only makes a person liable after slaughtering both a bull with its offspring and a sheep with its offspring. The word או teaches that each case is enough by itself. If או is busy with that, it is not free to include כלאים.

keyTerms.meaning: To separate, to teach that each item counts by itself
It is needed for something else
It would have entered your mind, a mistaken first thought
It comes to teach us

phrases.english: This 'or' is needed to separate,
for it would enter your mind to say:
until he slaughters a bull and its offspring
and a sheep and its offspring, he is not liable;
it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 2 by giving או a different job.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A word that is needed for one teaching is not free for a second teaching, and או is needed לחלק.

steps.title: Separating is learned from 'its offspring'
steps.stepSummary: The fact that each animal counts by itself is learned from the singular word בנו, so או stays free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the teaching of לחלק comes from a different word, בנו ('its offspring'), so או is still free to include כלאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה says בנו in the singular, 'its offspring,' and not 'their offspring.' That shows each animal is judged with its own offspring by itself. So לחלק does not need או.

keyTerms.meaning: Its offspring, in the singular
It is learned from, it comes out of

phrases.english: Separating is derived from 'its offspring.'
phrases.notes: The point is the singular: the Torah says 'its offspring,' not 'their offspring.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 3 by moving לחלק to the word בנו.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the teaching to a different word
steps.terutzMaskana: לחלק comes from בנו, so או is free to include כלאים.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to use 'or' for another teaching
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that one need not slaughter both a bull and a sheep with an offspring, and it seems to learn this from או.
steps.simpleTranslation: But 'or' is still needed for what a ברייתא teaches: if the Torah had said 'a bull and a sheep and its offspring,' I would think he is liable only if he slaughters a bull, a sheep, and the offspring. So the פסוק says 'a bull or a sheep, it and its offspring.' Isn't this learned from 'or'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again with a ברייתא. The ברייתא seems to use או to teach that a person does not need to slaughter both a bull and a sheep along with an offspring to be liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Had the תורה written 'שור ושה ובנו,' one might think liability needs all three animals. The ברייתא quotes 'שור או שה אותו ואת בנו' to reject that. If the ברייתא learns this from או, then או is busy again and cannot include כלאים.

keyTerms.meaning: Still, even so
Therefore the פסוק says, introducing the source
Is it not so that, a question that suggests the answer

phrases.english: But it is still needed for that which is taught in a ברייתא:
If it had said 'a bull and a sheep and its offspring,'
I would have said:
not until he slaughters a bull, a sheep, and its offspring;
therefore the verse says:
'A bull or a sheep, it and its offspring.'
Is it not from 'or' that he derives it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 4 freed או from לחלק, this step finds another job for או in a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא seems to use או to teach that a bull and a sheep are not both required, so או is not extra.

steps.title: The ברייתא learns it from 'it'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא learns its teaching from the word אותו, not from או.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא does not learn its teaching from או, but from the word אותו ('it').
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אותו points to one single animal with its offspring, so there is no need for both a bull and a sheep. That teaching comes from אותו, so או stays free to include כלאים.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It,' meaning one single parent animal

phrases.english: No, it is derived from 'it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 5 by moving the ברייתא's teaching to the word אותו.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the teaching to a different word
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא learns from אותו, so או still includes כלאים.

steps.title: What about חנניה, who uses 'it' for something else?
steps.stepSummary: This works for the רבנן, for whom אותו is extra. But חנניה uses אותו for another teaching, so where does he learn לחלק from?
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for the רבנן, for whom 'it' is extra. But for חנניה, for whom 'it' is not extra, where does he learn separating from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last answer. Moving the teaching to אותו only works for the רבנן, who have אותו free; חנניה uses אותו for something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For חנניה, אותו is already busy, so the ברייתא's teaching cannot come from it. Then או would be needed for that teaching, and the גמרא asks where חנניה learns that each animal counts by itself. The גמרא is making sure the whole system works for both opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well, introducing 'but what about the other opinion'
Extra, free to teach something new
From where does he learn it?

steps.confusionAlert: Steps 11-19 explain the disagreement between the רבנן and חנניה and how the רבנן read אותו and בנו. For now, just know that the רבנן have אותו free and חנניה does not.

phrases.english: This works well according to the Rabbis,
for whom 'it' is extra;
but according to Chananya,
for whom 'it' is not extra,
from where does he derive separating?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְרַבָּנַן דִּמְיַיתַּר לְהוּ אוֹתוֹ אֶלָּא לַחֲנַנְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the answer of step 6 against the opinion of חנניה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the teaching comes from אותו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For חנניה, אותו is not free, so או would be needed for that teaching, leaving no source for כלאים.

steps.title: חנניה needs no פסוק because he follows רבי יונתן
steps.stepSummary: חנניה does not need a פסוק for לחלק, because he holds like רבי יונתן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Separating does not need a פסוק, because he holds like רבי יונתן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that חנניה does not need any special word to teach לחלק, because he follows the approach of רבי יונתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יונתן holds that when a פסוק lists several items, each one counts by itself unless the תורה says they go together. So for חנניה, a bull alone or a sheep alone is already enough without any extra word, and או stays free to include כלאים.

keyTerms.meaning: No פסוק is needed for this
He holds like, he agrees with the opinion of

steps.whatToRemember: According to everyone, או includes כלאים in אותו ואת בנו. For the רבנן, the other teachings come from בנו and אותו. For חנניה, לחלק needs no פסוק at all because he holds like רבי יונתן.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that אותו ואת בנו applies to כלאים according to both the רבנן and חנניה, even though each gets there in a different way.

phrases.english: Separating does not need a verse,
for he holds like Rabbi Yonatan.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְחַלֵּק לָא צְרִיךְ קְרָא דְּסָבַר לַהּ כְּרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 by showing that חנניה needs no פסוק for לחלק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Removes the need for a source by using a general rule of reading פסוקים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: חנניה needs או for לחלק, so או is not free for כלאים.
steps.terutzMaskana: Following רבי יונתן, חנניה gets לחלק without a פסוק, so או includes כלאים for him too.

steps.title: The ברייתא about cursing father and mother: רבי יאשיה's view
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי יאשיה needs an extra phrase in the פסוק to teach that cursing just one parent is punishable.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: 'A man who curses his father and his mother.' From this alone I would only know about cursing both together. How do I know that cursing only his father, or only his mother, counts? The פסוק later says 'his father and his mother he cursed.' This means he cursed his father, or he cursed his mother. These are the words of רבי יאשיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up the last step, that חנניה holds like רבי יונתן. First it quotes the view of רבי יאשיה, which sets up the contrast with רבי יונתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יאשיה, the word 'and' on its own means both together. So he needs a second phrase in the פסוק to teach that each parent counts alone. This shows the opposite view from רבי יונתן, which the גמרא brings next.

keyTerms.meaning: I would only know (this case), from the plain פסוק
From where do we know?
The פסוק teaches (by saying)
One who curses his father and mother

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: ״אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יְקַלֵּל אֶת אָבִיו וְאֶת אִמּוֹ״,
phrases.english: As it is taught: "A man who curses his father and his mother"
I would only know about his father and his mother (both together)
His father without his mother,
and his mother without his father, from where do we know?
The verse says: "His father and his mother he cursed"
He cursed his father, he cursed his mother.
phrases.notes: He reads it as two separate cases, so cursing either parent alone is enough.

phrases.english: These are the words of Rabbi Yoshiya.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: ״אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יְקַלֵּל אֶת אָבִיו וְאֶת אִמּוֹ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for the רבי יונתן position mentioned in Step 8, starting with the opposing view of רבי יאשיה.
steps.raayaObject: That there is a known מחלוקת about whether 'and' means each one alone, which explains how חנניה can do without a פסוק for לחלק.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on מקלל אביו ואמו (ויקרא 20:9).

steps.title: רבי יונתן: 'and' already means each one alone
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן says 'his father and his mother' already covers both together and each one alone, unless the פסוק says 'together'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן says: The words mean both of them together, and they also mean each one by itself, unless the פסוק specifically tells you 'together'.
steps.whatsHappening: Now the ברייתא gives רבי יונתן's view, which is the real point the גמרא needs. This explains why חנניה does not need a פסוק for לחלק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יונתן, 'and' automatically includes each item alone. Only the word 'together' limits it to both at once. So for חנניה, who holds like רבי יונתן, 'a bull and a sheep' would already mean each animal counts separately, and the word או is left free for his own teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: It implies / it means
Both of them together
One by itself
Together: the word that limits a law to both at once

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יונתן: 'and' means both together and each alone, unless the פסוק says 'together'. Because חנניה holds like him, he needs no פסוק for לחלק.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two: רבי יאשיה needs an extra phrase to split the items, while רבי יונתן gets the split for free from the word 'and' itself.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a famous general rule about how to read 'and' in the תורה, used in many סוגיות.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yonatan says:
It means both of them together,
and it also means each one by itself,
unless the verse spells out for you "together."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן אוֹמֵר: מַשְׁמָע שְׁנֵיהֶם כְּאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא begun in Step 9 by giving the view of רבי יונתן, which supports the answer of Step 8.
steps.raayaObject: That חנניה, holding like רבי יונתן, gets לחלק from the word 'and' and needs no פסוק.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יונתן's statement in the ברייתא of מקלל אביו ואמו.

steps.title: What exactly are the views of חנניה and the רבנן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the מחלוקת between חנניה and the רבנן actually is.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the view of חנניה, and what is the view of the רבנן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask what חנניה and the רבנן, mentioned earlier, actually argue about. This sets up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier steps said חנניה uses אותו for something else while the רבנן have it free. Now the גמרא wants to know the actual מחלוקת behind that.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages, the majority view

phrases.english: What is Chananya's view, and what is the Rabbis' view?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the source discussion to clarify the two opinions named in Step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The content of the מחלוקת between חנניה and the רבנן.

steps.title: Does אותו ואת בנו apply to males too?
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן say אותו ואת בנו applies only to females. חנניה says it applies to males and females.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: אותו ואת בנו applies to females and not to males. חנניה says it applies to both males and females.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא. The רבנן limit the איסור to a mother and its young, and חנניה includes a father and its young too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether you may slaughter a father animal and its offspring on the same day. The רבנן allow it, since only the mother counts. חנניה forbids it, since he applies the איסור to males as well.

keyTerms.meaning: The איסור against slaughtering an animal and its offspring on the same day
Applies
Females
Males

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: אוֹתוֹ וְאֶת בְּנוֹ נוֹהֵג בִּנְקֵבוֹת,
phrases.english: As it is taught: "Itself and its offspring" applies to females,
and does not apply to males.
phrases.notes: He means a father animal together with its offspring.

phrases.english: Chananya says:
It applies both to males and to females.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: אוֹתוֹ וְאֶת בְּנוֹ נוֹהֵג בִּנְקֵבוֹת
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבנן: only females (a mother and its young). חנניה: both males and females.

steps.title: What is the reason of the רבנן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the רבנן limit אותו ואת בנו to females.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the רבנן?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the רבנן's view. This sets up another ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק itself is written in a masculine form ('אותו', 'בנו'), so limiting it to females needs an explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason of the Rabbis?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the רבנן's ruling stated in Step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source or reasoning for limiting אותו ואת בנו to females.

steps.title: Comparing אותו ואת בנו to the mother bird
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא compares אותו ואת בנו to שילוח הקן. Just as that מצוה is only with a mother bird, this איסור should be only with a mother animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: One might think אותו ואת בנו applies to both males and females. But it is logical: The תורה obligated here, and it obligated with a mother bird on its young. Just as with the mother bird it is females and not males, so too here it is females and not males.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives the רבנן a logical argument. It compares אותו ואת בנו to the mother bird of שילוח הקן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both laws deal with a parent and its young. The law of the bird clearly speaks only of the mother, so the ברייתא argues that the animal law should also be only about the mother. This is a דין, a reasoning argument, and not a direct reading of a פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: One might have thought
And it is logical: introduces a reasoning argument
A mother bird sitting on its young (the law of שילוח הקן)
Just as... so too: the form of a comparison

steps.confusionAlert: The 'one might think' (יכול) is the side being pushed away. The ברייתא's own argument is the comparison that follows, which limits the law to females.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: יָכוֹל יְהֵא אוֹתוֹ וְאֶת בְּנוֹ
phrases.english: As it is taught: One might think that "itself and its offspring"
applies both to males and to females?
But it is logical:
The Torah obligated here,
and it obligated with a mother upon its young;
phrases.notes: This is the mother bird you must send away before taking the chicks (דברים 22:6).

phrases.english: Just as when it obligated with a mother upon its young,
it is with females and not with males,
so too when it obligated here,
it is with females and not with males.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: יָכוֹל יְהֵא אוֹתוֹ וְאֶת בְּנוֹ נוֹהֵג בֵּין בִּזְכָרִים וּבֵין בִּנְקֵבוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 13 with a ברייתא giving the reasoning of the רבנן.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A logical comparison to אם על הבנים: just as that law is only with the mother, so is אותו ואת בנו.

steps.title: The comparison to the mother bird is challenged
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא pushes back on its own comparison: שילוח הקן does not apply to birds you already own, but אותו ואת בנו applies even to animals you own, so the two laws are not alike.
steps.simpleTranslation: No! You can say this about the mother bird and her chicks, because there the תורה did not treat birds you already have the same as birds you just find. But can you say the same about an animal and its offspring, where the תורה did treat animals you already have the same as ones you don't?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא challenges the comparison it just made between אותו ואת בנו and שילוח הקן. It argues that the two laws are too different to learn one from the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שילוח הקן applies only to a nest you happen to come across, not to birds already in your possession. אותו ואת בנו applies even to your own animals that are ready for slaughter. Since the second law is broader in this way, maybe it is also broader and covers males too.

keyTerms.meaning: No, if you say... (a formula that rejects a comparison by showing a difference)
A mother bird sitting on her young (the case of שילוח הקן)
Prepared or ready: something already in your possession
Like what is not prepared: something you just happen to find

steps.confusionAlert: This challenge is part of the ברייתא itself. The ברייתא is testing its own comparison before it defends it. It is not a new opinion arguing with the רבנן.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא, אִם אָמַרְתָּ בְּאֵם עַל הַבָּנִים,
phrases.english: No, if you say so regarding a mother bird with her young,
since [the Torah] did not make, with it,
prepared ones like unprepared ones,
phrases.notes: He means birds you already own don't count. שילוח הקן only applies to a nest you happen upon.

where [the Torah] made prepared ones like unprepared ones?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the comparison to שילוח הקן brought in Step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the comparison between אותו ואת בנו and שילוח הקן.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The two laws differ: שילוח הקן excludes birds you own, while אותו ואת בנו includes animals you own. So they cannot be fully compared.

steps.title: The word 'אותו' saves the comparison
steps.stepSummary: The word 'אותו' shows the איסור applies to one parent, not two. Once the פסוק has made this split, the comparison to שילוח הקן works again: only females.
steps.simpleTranslation: So the פסוק says 'אותו' (it): one and not two. Once the פסוק split them apart, I can go back to my comparison: the תורה obligated here, and it obligated with the mother bird. Just as with the mother bird the law is for females and not males, so too here it is for females and not males.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the challenge with a word in the פסוק. 'אותו' teaches that only one parent is included, and that brings back the comparison to the mother bird.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge was that the two laws are not alike. The word 'אותו' shows the תורה meant only one of the two parents. With that settled, the ברייתא can rely on the comparison again: both laws are about the mother.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק teaches (introduces a proof from the words of a פסוק)
One and not two
The פסוק separated (split the two parents apart)
I have earned the right to go back to my logical comparison
Females / males

steps.whatToRemember: According to the רבנן, the word 'אותו' (only one parent) together with the comparison to שילוח הקן limits אותו ואת בנו to the mother.

phrases.english: The verse teaches: 'it'
one and not two.
After the verse separated them, I may return to my reasoning:

phrases.aramaic: חִיֵּיב כָּאן וְחִיֵּיב בְּאֵם עַל הַבָּנִים –

Just as when it obligated with the mother bird on her young,
it is with females and not with males,
so too when it obligated here,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 15 and brings back the comparison.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual proof from the word 'אותו' that lets the comparison stand.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the laws differ about owned animals, maybe אותו ואת בנו also covers males.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'אותו' means only one parent, so the comparison holds: only females.

steps.title: A backup proof from 'בנו'
steps.stepSummary: If you want to object, there is another proof: 'בנו' points to the parent whose young follows it, which leaves out the male.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want to argue, the פסוק says 'בנו' (its offspring): this means the parent whose offspring is attached to it. That leaves out the male, whose offspring is not attached to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a second proof, in case someone still objects. The word 'בנו' shows the law is about the mother.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The young animal stays close to its mother, not its father. So 'its offspring' naturally describes the mother's relationship. This backs up the conclusion that males are left out.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish to say (if you want to object)
Attached to it, following after it
Leaves out, excludes

phrases.english: And if you wish to say [otherwise]: 'its offspring'
means the one whose offspring is attached to it,

phrases.english: which excludes a male, whose offspring is not attached to it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Heads off a possible objection to the 'אותו' derivation of Step 16 (which parent is the 'one'?) by bringing proof from 'בנו'. Steps 18-19 spell out that objection.
steps.raayaObject: That אותו ואת בנו applies only to the mother.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word 'בנו' in ויקרא 22:28: the parent whose young follows it.

steps.title: What objection is 'אם נפשך לומר' answering?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what objection the phrase 'if you wish to say' is referring to.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the 'if you wish to say' about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask a clarifying question about the ברייתא's wording. It is setting up the next step, where it will explain the hidden objection.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said 'if you wish to say' but never stated the objection. The גמרא wants to know what someone might have argued that made the 'בנו' proof necessary.

keyTerms.meaning: What? (asking what something refers to)

phrases.english: What is 'if you wish to say'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the unclear phrase in Step 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which objection the 'בנו' proof is meant to answer.

steps.title: The objection: 'אותו' sounds masculine
steps.stepSummary: Someone might say 'אותו' is a masculine word and so means a male. The answer is that 'בנו' points to the parent the young follows, which leaves out the male.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say 'אותו' sounds like it means a male, the פסוק also says 'בנו': the one whose offspring is attached to it. That leaves out the male, whose offspring is not attached to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the hidden objection. 'אותו' limits the law to one parent, and since 'אותו' is a masculine word, maybe that one parent is the male and not the female. The word 'בנו' answers that objection.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אותו' taught that only one parent is meant. Its masculine grammar could suggest that this one parent is the male. 'בנו' shows the focus is on the parent the young stays with, which is the mother. So the רבנן's position stands: only females.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (introduces a possible objection)
Implies a male
But the פסוק says

steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן limit אותו ואת בנו to females using two proofs: the comparison to שילוח הקן (with 'אותו'), and 'בנו', the parent whose young follows it. 'בנו' also answers the idea that the masculine 'אותו' means a male.
steps.confusionAlert: The worry is not that males are added alongside females. It is that 'אותו', which picks out just one parent, might pick the male. 'בנו' shows that the one parent is the mother.

phrases.english: which excludes a male, whose offspring is not attached to it.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The objection is that 'אותו' sounds masculine. 'בנו' answers it by pointing to the mother, whom the young follows.
